summary: Specifies version 5 of Kerberos, a network authentication system where a trusted server issues tickets so users and services can prove their identity to each other without sending passwords over the network. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 4120, RFC 6649.

eli5.summary: A trusted ticket booth hands you a pass to get into rides. You show the pass, not your wallet, so nobody can steal your money.

questions: what is cross-realm authentication in kerberos
subtitle: How a trusted server proves users are who they say they are without sending passwords over the network.

tldr.problem: Users need to prove their identity to network services without sending passwords over an open network, and services need to know that a user is legitimate without trusting the user's computer or network.
tldr.mechanism: Kerberos uses a trusted authentication server to issue time-limited encrypted tickets. A client proves it has a user's secret key (password-derived) to get a ticket-granting ticket, then uses that to get service tickets without further passwords. Each ticket is encrypted in the target server's key so only that server can read it.
tldr.outcome: Services can verify a user's identity cryptographically without needing direct access to passwords, and users can authenticate once then get credentials for many services. RFC 4120 and RFC 6649 replaced this document as standards.

facts.label: Ticket lifetime
facts.value: Limited by client, server, and realm policy

facts.label: Session key
facts.value: Random, time-limited, shared between client and server

today: RFC 1510 is Historic. RFC 4120 and RFC 6649 updated and clarified the Kerberos V5 specification. Kerberos remains widely deployed in enterprise networks for authentication.

sections.title: The Authentication Problem
sections.content:
Kerberos is a network authentication system where a trusted server lets principals (users or services) prove their identities to each other without sending passwords over the network. The system assumes that an attacker can read, modify, and insert messages on the network, and that each host's clock is loosely synchronized.

The core idea is delegation: a client authenticates once to a Kerberos server (the KDC, or Key Distribution Center) using its secret key (derived from a password), and the server gives the client time-limited credentials in the form of encrypted tickets. The client can then present these tickets to services without ever revealing its password. The authentication server does not need to verify that the request comes from the named principal; instead, the reply is encrypted in that principal's key, so only they can decrypt it and use it.
sections.eli5: You don't need to show your real ID to every store. You get a ticket from a trusted booth, and the ticket proves you are who you say. You show the ticket, not your password.

sections.title: Tickets and Credentials
sections.content:
A ticket is a record that includes the client's identity, a session key (a temporary encryption key), a timestamp, and other information, all encrypted in the target server's key. A ticket only proves the client's identity when presented with an authenticator: a structure encrypted in the session key that includes a timestamp, proving it was just created.

Kerberos supports several ticket types, controlled by flags. An initial ticket (marked INITIAL) is issued directly by the authentication server when the user provides a password. A ticket-granting ticket (TGT) is a special initial ticket for the Ticket-Granting Service (TGS), which issues service tickets without requiring the user's password again. Renewable tickets can be extended by the KDC without re-issuing. Forwardable tickets can be used on behalf of a user on a different host. Postdated tickets are marked INVALID until a future start time, useful for batch jobs.
sections.eli5: A ticket says "This person is Alice and can talk to the file server, and here is a secret code Alice and the file server both know." The secret code proves Alice made the ticket just now, not long ago.

sections.title: The Three Key Exchanges
sections.content:
Kerberos uses three message exchanges to establish authentication. The first is the Authentication Service (AS) exchange. The client sends a cleartext request with its identity and the server it wants credentials for. The server looks up the client's secret key, generates a random session key, and returns a ticket for the target server plus the session key, all encrypted in the client's secret key. The client decrypts this with its password-derived key, verifies the nonce (a random number sent in the request) to detect replays, and stores the ticket and session key.

The second is the Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) exchange. Instead of sending a password-derived key, the client sends the ticket-granting ticket and an authenticator encrypted in the TGT's session key. The TGS verifies that the authenticator is fresh (the timestamp is close to current time) and the ticket has not expired, then issues a new ticket for the requested service. This allows a user to get many service tickets without re-entering a password.

The third is the Client/Server (AP) exchange. The client sends the service ticket plus an authenticator encrypted in the service's session key. The server decrypts the ticket (it knows the session key because it is sealed in the ticket), verifies the authenticator is fresh, and optionally sends back its own authenticator to prove it decrypted the ticket correctly. The shared session key can then be used to protect further communication.
sections.eli5: First, you go to the ticket booth with your password and get a master pass. Second, you show the master pass to get a pass for the library. Third, you show the library pass to the librarian, who confirms it is real.

sections.title: Encryption and Cross-Realm Trust
sections.content:
All sensitive information in Kerberos tickets and messages is encrypted using shared secret keys. Each principal (user or service) shares a secret key with the KDC. Session keys are random and time-limited, so stealing one compromises only recent or current communication. The protocol uses various encryption methods (DES, MD5, and others) and checksums to detect tampering.

Kerberos supports authentication across organizational boundaries through inter-realm keys. If two realms (organizations) share a secret key, the KDC of one realm can act as a client to the other realm's TGS. A user in one realm can request a ticket to a service in another realm. The TGS consults an authentication path (a sequence of intermediate realms) to route the request, and each realm along the path adds itself to a transited field in the final ticket, so the service knows which realms were involved.

Kerberos has important limitations. It does not prevent denial-of-service attacks: an attacker can prevent a client from reaching the KDC or a server. If a principal's secret key is stolen, an attacker can masquerade as that principal. Password-guessing attacks are possible if a user chooses a weak password. Host clocks must be loosely synchronized or the timestamp check will fail.
sections.eli5: All secrets are encrypted so attackers cannot read them. Different organizations can trust each other by sharing a secret. But if you use a weak password, an attacker can guess it. And if your clock is too far from others, nothing works.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content: RFC 1510 was the first formal specification of Kerberos V5 and saw wide deployment in the 1990s and 2000s. However, it was written as an Internet Standard at a time when the specification could be clearer. RFC 4120 (published in 2005) consolidated the Kerberos V5 specification and clarified ambiguities. RFC 6649 (2012) deprecated the use of single DES encryption in Kerberos.
sections.eli5: This was the official rule book for Kerberos Version 5. Newer books (RFCs 4120 and 6649) fixed unclear parts and added security updates.
